title: Validation Basics
description: Learn how to validate input data in ASP.NET Core Web API.

data.text: **Input validation** is the foundation of any reliable HTTP API. Without it, malformed or malicious data can reach your domain layer, corrupt your database, or expose security flaws. ASP.NET Core provides built-in data annotation attributes that let you declare rules directly on your model and have the framework enforce them automatically.

terms.definition: Attributes placed on model properties that describe validation rules such as required, length, range, and format constraints.
A dictionary that holds the result of model binding and validation. The [ApiController] attribute checks ModelState.IsValid automatically before actions run.
The base class for all built-in attributes. You can subclass it to create custom validation logic for business rules.
An interface that lets a model validate itself as a whole, enabling cross-property rules that single attributes cannot express.

data.text: Validating at the boundary of your application — inside controllers or middleware — keeps invalid data out of your services and repositories. This protects business invariants, simplifies error reporting, and gives clients fast, descriptive feedback before any expensive work runs.

data.caption: How a request flows through ASP.NET Core validation.

flowchart TB

  B --> G[JSON Deserialization]

data.text: Define a request DTO with validation attributes. The framework will run them after model binding but before your action executes when the controller is decorated with [ApiController].

data.title: Validation Attributes on a Request DTO
data.content: Decorating properties with [Required], [StringLength], [Range], and [EmailAddress] enforces rules before the action runs.

data.title: ModelState Is Automatic with [ApiController]
data.text: When a controller is annotated with [ApiController], ASP.NET Core automatically returns a 400 Bad Request with RFC 7807 ProblemDetails whenever ModelState.IsValid is false. You do not need to check it manually in every action.
If you are not using [ApiController] (for example, in a minimal API without the attribute), you can still inspect ModelState and short-circuit the request with a 400 response.

data.content: Returning a ValidationProblem when ModelState is invalid.

data.title: Don't Skip Server Validation
data.text: Client-side validation improves UX, but it can be bypassed. Always enforce the same rules on the server; otherwise attackers can submit invalid data directly with curl or Postman.

data.title: Validate a Product DTO
data.description: Create a CreateProductRequest DTO with strict validation rules and test it with an invalid payload.
steps: Create a CreateProductRequest class with Name, SKU, Price, and ReleaseDate.
Annotate SKU with [RegularExpression] matching three uppercase letters followed by four digits, e.g. ABC1234.
Annotate ReleaseDate with a custom ValidationAttribute that disallows dates in the past.
POST a payload that violates each rule and confirm the API returns 400 with field-level errors.
data.expectedOutcome: An API that rejects bad input with descriptive ProblemDetails and accepts well-formed requests with 201 Created.

items.text: Every public request DTO has [Required] on string properties
String and collection properties have explicit maximum length
Numeric ranges use [Range] rather than manual checks
Custom business rules live in a reusable ValidationAttribute
Controllers use [ApiController] so ModelState is automatic

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use data annotations to declare rules directly on properties
[ApiController] checks ModelState.IsValid before the action runs
Invalid models automatically produce RFC 7807 ProblemDetails
Custom ValidationAttribute encapsulates complex, reusable rules
Always validate on the server, even when the client validates
data.takeaway: Validate at the boundary so your domain layer can trust the data it receives.
